## Presentation outline

- Summary of Tanaskovi'c et al. (2012), Motivation - Hamish
- Our data on Serbian spa waters - Cathrine
- Results of data analysis:
  - Normality tests - Jack
  - Samples consistency - Hamish
  - Correlations, PCA, Factor, cluster analysis - Viktor
  - Hierarchical Cluster Analysis - Cathrine
- Conclusions - Jack

## The Report

- Sampled spa water from 30 locations across Serbia.

- Measured 18 variables from 4 types of geological structure.

- 12 hydrochemical variables.

- 6 Radioactive Isotopes.

- Aimed to classify and group spa waters based on hydrochemical properties, radioactive isotopes, and geological structure.

- Analysed the data using Pearson correlation, PCA, and HCA.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Our Analysis

We aimed to answer the following questions about the hydrological data using quantitative and qualitative analysis methods.

- Can you improve the paper’s results using Factor Analysis in terms of model quality with parsimony?

- Are the groups identified by the dendrogram consistent with changes in the linkage and distance?

```{r data-read-jack}

data <- read.csv(file.path("..","..","Data","Hydrochemical Data.csv"), header=TRUE)

hydroclean<-data[-1, 3:14]
as.numeric(hydroclean$T)->hydroclean$T
as.numeric(hydroclean$EC)->hydroclean$EC
as.numeric(hydroclean$TS)->hydroclean$TS
as.numeric(hydroclean$Ca2.)->hydroclean$Ca2.
as.numeric(hydroclean$SO4_2.)->hydroclean$SO4_2.

library(MASS)

trhydroclean <- hydroclean

for (col_name in names(hydroclean)) {
  x <- hydroclean[[col_name]] 
  #Make sure we have only strictly positive values
  if (any(x <= 0, na.rm = TRUE)) {
    x <- x + 0.001 
  }
  
  #Get optimal lambda for the column we are in for its BC transform
  bc <- boxcox(lm(x ~ 1), plotit = FALSE)
  optimal_lambda <- bc$x[which.max(bc$y)]
  
  #Apply the BC transform to this column
  if (abs(optimal_lambda) < 1e-3) {
    trhydroclean[[col_name]] <- log(x)
  } else {
    trhydroclean[[col_name]] <- (x^optimal_lambda - 1) / optimal_lambda
  }
  
}
```

## Shapiro-Wilk Tests 3

Shapiro-Wilk tests are used to test univariate normality

Our Shapiro-Wilk tests conclude non-normality for all our variables (at 0.05 significance level)

The chlorine ion measure (Cl.) gets the smallest p-value = $1.566\times10^{-10}$

The calcium ion variable (Ca2.) gets the largest p-value = 0.02344

## Multivariate Normal Tests

Because we have variables that individually don't follow a normal distribution our joint distribution can not be multivariate normal

In Tanaskovic et al., where data failed on the Shapiro-Wilk tests, a Box-Cox transformation was used

If we do the same we won't be guaranteed a joint multivariate normal distribution but we can try

## Transformed Variables

This transformation has improved the look of our histograms and normal QQ-plots

All of our p-values have increased to above our 0.05 significance level and so we fail to reject the null hypothesis and conclude that each of our transformed variables follow a normal distribution

## Multivariate Normal Tests 2

```{r, echo=FALSE}
library(psych)
mardia(trhydroclean, plot=FALSE)
```

Mardia's test has the null hypothesis the data follows a multivariate normal distribution and looks at two features of the data: skewness and kurtosis

We get a p-value of 0.79 for skewness and 0.038 for kurtosis

Because we reject for the kurtosis component we reject the null hypothesis of the test - even with transformed variables the data is not multivariate normal

## Multivariate Normal Tests 3

```{r}
library(mvnTest)
HZ.test(trhydroclean)
```

## Samples Consistency Analysis

### Key Findings - Mahalanobis

- 10 surprising observations past the first two cut points.

- 5 past all three.

- Observations: 1, 2, 4, 15, 16, 23, 24, 28, 29 and 30.

```{r mahalanobis-setup, Echo = FALSE}

mu.hat <- colMeans(data_spa_waters_raw)
Sigma.hat <- cov(data_spa_waters_raw)

dM <- mahalanobis(data_spa_waters_raw, center = mu.hat, cov = Sigma.hat)

upper.quantiles <- qchisq(c(.9, .95, .99), df = 9)
density.at.quantiles <- dchisq(x = upper.quantiles, df = 9)
cut.points <- data.frame(upper.quantiles, density.at.quantiles)
```

```{r mahalanobis-plot, echo = FALSE, fig.width=6, fig.height=6}

ggplot(data.frame(dM), aes(x = dM)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = nclass.FD(dM),
                 fill = "white", col = "black") +
  geom_rug() +
  stat_function(fun = dchisq, args = list(df = 9),
                col = "red", size = 2, alpha = .7, xlim = c(0, 25)) +
  geom_segment(data = cut.points,
               aes(x = upper.quantiles, xend = upper.quantiles,
                   y = rep(0, 3), yend = density.at.quantiles),
               col = "blue", size = 2) +
  xlab("Mahalanobis distances and cut points") +
  ylab("Histogram and density")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Key Findings - Pairs Plot

- Strong positive relationship between EC and TS.

- $Cl^-$ and $Mg^{2+}$ have high right-skew.

- Difference in EC and TS values across surprise levels.

```{r surprise-classification}

data_spa_waters_raw$dM <- dM
data_spa_waters_raw$surprise <- cut(
  data_spa_waters_raw$dM,
  breaks = c(0, upper.quantiles, Inf),
  labels = c("Typical", "Somewhat", "Surprising", "Very")
)
```

```{r pairs-plot-surprise, fig.width=9, fig.height=9}

ggpairs(data_spa_waters_raw, columns = 1:9,
        ggplot2::aes(col = surprise, alpha = .5),
        upper = list(continuous = "density", combo = "box_no_facet")) +
  ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = c("lightgray", "green", "blue", "red")) +
  ggplot2::theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1))
```

## PCA {.smaller}

```{r pca-reset-raw, fig.height=3, fig.width=4}

data_spa_waters_raw <- data_spa_waters_classes[, -c(ncolumns_data_spa_waters_classes - 1, ncolumns_data_spa_waters_classes)]

PCA.data_spa_waters_raw <- prcomp(data_spa_waters_raw, center = TRUE, scale = TRUE)
plot(PCA.data_spa_waters_raw, type = "l")
```

4 PCs: 74.727% of the cumulative variance in the data, just under three quarters, with PC1 explaining 35.1%, PC2 17.5%, PC3 12,4% and PC4 9.74% of the total variance.

## PCA - Structure

```{r biplot-geological-structure, fig.height=4, fig.width=6}
ggbiplot(PCA.data_spa_waters_raw, obs.scale = 1, var.scale = 1,
         groups = interaction(data_spa_waters_classes$Geological.structure), ellipse = TRUE)
```

```{r biplot-geological-region, fig.height=4, fig.width=6}

```

## Factor analysis {.smaller}

```{r factanal-diagram}

fa.diagram(factanal(data_spa_waters_raw, factors = 4)$loadings, digits = 3)
```

Four factors explain 64.9% of variation in the data. No single factor explains a large portion of variation.

## Factor analysis - with PCA {.smaller}

```{r principal-varimax}

fa_result <- principal(data_spa_waters_raw, nfactors = 4, rotate = "varimax")

# Check variance accounted for by each rotated factor

fa.diagram(principal(data_spa_waters_raw, nfactors = 4, rotate = "varimax")$loadings, digits = 3)
```

Maintains the 74.73% total variance. These loadings are the closest to the ones described in the paper.

## Cluster analysis - Structure

```{r clustering-kmeans geom, fig.height=4, fig.width=6}

# Build the scores data frame
scores_df <- as.data.frame(PCA.data_spa_waters_raw$x)
scores_df$Group <- data_spa_waters_classes$Geological.structure #Region
scores_df$Label <- 1:nrow(scores_df)

# Variance explained for axis labels
var_explained <- (PCA.data_spa_waters_raw$sdev^2 / sum(PCA.data_spa_waters_raw$sdev^2)) * 100

# Run clustering on the PC scores
k <- 2
km <- kmeans(scores_df[, c("PC1", "PC2")], centers = k, nstart=20)
scores_df$Cluster <- factor(km$cluster)

# Dynamic color/shape mapping for Group
groups <- unique(scores_df$Group)
my_colors <- setNames(c("magenta", "blue", "black", "red", "darkgreen", "orange")[1:length(groups)], groups)
my_shapes <- setNames(c(8, 16, 0, 2, 17, 15)[1:length(groups)], groups)

ggplot(scores_df, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2)) +
  stat_ellipse(aes(group = Cluster), type = "norm", level = 0.95,
               color = "grey30", linetype = 2, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(color = Group, shape = Group), size = 3, stroke = 1.2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = Label, color = Group), vjust = -0.8, hjust = 0.5,
            size = 3.5, fontface = "bold", show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  scale_color_manual(values = my_colors) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = my_shapes) +
  labs(x = paste0("Factor 1 (PC1) : ", round(var_explained[1], 2), "%"),
       y = paste0("Factor 2 (PC2) : ", round(var_explained[2], 2), "%")) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.title = element_blank(),
        legend.position = c(0.2, 0.85),
        legend.background = element_rect(color = "black", linewidth = 0.3))
```

## Dendrogram 1

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#Hierachical Clustering 
dist <- dist(X[ , c(4:8)] , diag=TRUE) 
hc <- hclust(dist)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#Dendrogram
dhc <- as.dendrogram(hc)                        

#Dendrogram colours
i=0
colLab<<-function(n){
  if(is.leaf(n)){
    a=attributes(n)
    m=match(attributes(n)$label,data[,1])
    
    #Zone Colours
    zone=data[m,16];
    if(zone=="Pannonian Basin"){col_zone="blue"};
    if(zone=="Vardar Zone"){col_zone="red"}; 
    if(zone=="Serbo-Macedonian Massif"){col_zone="darkgreen"}; 
    if(zone=="Carpatho-Balkans"){col_zone="purple"}
    
    #Structure Colours
    structure=data[m,15];
    if(structure=="Hydrogeological basin"){col_structure="lightblue"};
    if(structure=="Karstic terrains"){col_structure="pink"};
    if(structure=="Volcanogenic massifs"){col_structure="lightgreen"};
    if(structure=="Metamorphic regions"){col_structure="plum"} 
    
    #Leaf attributes
    attr(n,"nodePar")<-c(a$nodePar,list(cex=1.5,lab.cex=1,pch=20,col=col_structure,lab.col=col_zone,lab.font=1,lab.cex=1))
  }
  return(n)
}

dL <- dendrapply(dhc, colLab)

#Plot
plot(dL)

#Legend for zones
legend("topleft",
       legend = c("Pannonian Basin" , "Vardar Zone" , "Serbo-Macedonian Massif" , "Carpatho-Balkans"), 
       col = c("red", "blue" , "Darkgreen", "Purple"),
       pch = c(4,4,4,4), bty = "n",  pt.cex = 1.5, cex = 0.8,
       text.col = "black", horiz = FALSE,
       inset= c(0,0))

#Legend for structures      
legend("left",
       legend = c("Hydrogeological basin", "Karstic terrains", "Volcanogenic massifs", "Metamorphic regions"), 
       col = c("lightblue","pink", "lightgreen", "plum"),
       pch = c(20,20,20,20), bty = "n",  pt.cex = 1.5, cex = 0.8,
       text.col = "black", horiz = FALSE,
       inset= c(0,0))
```

## Tanaskovic et al.'s Principal Component Analysis

Their PCA reduced the variables to four latent factors which explained 74.2% of the sampling variance responsible for the data structure

The first component explained 37.5% variance and was made up of variables that meant it could be conditionally named the “mineralisation or residence time” factor

The second (the “hardness” component), third, and fourth principal components accounted for less variation: between 10.5% and 13.8%

## Our Factor Analysis

Tests for whether the specified factor model is sufficient to reproduce the observed correlation matrix gave us very small p-values for each model with one through four factors

Our FA does not yield a model that is more parsimonious than Tanaskovic et al.'s PCA while also providing an adequate fit to our data

So we can't improve the results of the paper with FA in terms of model parsimony

## Factor Analysis Advantage

Factor analysis does improve the interpretability of the underlying relationships between our variables

We get clear groups and also are able to identify variables not significantly explained by the factors

So the real answer is that we can not improve on Tanaskovic’s PCA but we can improve interpretability while retaining parsimony

## Dendrograms

The green and purple groups have a higher merge point, suggesting they are more dissimilar

The red and blue groups on the other hand have a lower merge point, meaning they are more similar to each other than the green and purple group

The final merge is a big jump from the two main branches which suggests the two branches identified before this are very dissimilar

The groups identified by the dendrogram are fairly consistent with the changes in linkage and distance
